candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

The fallen Watchers ask Enoch to intercede for them: 'They had not the power to speak with Him or to lift up their eyes to heaven for shame of their sins for which they had been condemned' — the inability of the fallen to face God directly. The shame-condition Tewahedo reads as the inverse of the elect's privileged direct address to God (cf. Heb 4:16 'come boldly unto the throne of grace'): unrepented sin produces moral inability to approach, even apart from any external prohibition. The Tewahedo confessional-sacramental theology reads this as the textual basis for the priest's mediating role in sin-burdened conscience.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

After Enoch's attempted intercession, the divine response: 'And the vision was shown to me thus: Behold, in the vision clouds invited me and a mist summoned me' — the prelude to God's denial of forgiveness for the fallen Watchers. The denial itself comes in chs 14-16: the Watchers' rebellion is not forgivable because they sinned with full angelic knowledge, where humans sin with partial knowledge. Tewahedo theological tradition draws explicit distinction: human sin is fully redeemable through Christ's incarnation (the Word assumed human nature); angelic sin is not (the Word did not assume angelic nature). The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok grounds this distinction textually.
